ISG's survey of 300 G2000 executives (Oct-Nov 2024) reports only that AI is 30% of the 2025 budget increase and AI spend grows 5.7% vs 1.8% for IT, not the level share. Related estimates disagree by far more than a factor of 2: Oxford Economics puts AI under 4% of enterprise tech spend in 2025 (all enterprises, model-based); BCG AI Radar has large firms planning AI spend of about 5% of revenue, which would be comparable to or above typical IT budgets. Under D23 (scope not matched; estimates span >2x) this stays ungradable, though every estimate found sits well below 40%.

Still ungradable (D22). Qualitative, universal claim ('all enterprises') with no public measure of stop-gap measures or of their effect on cloud-economics goals. GPU scarcity in 2024 is anecdotal support only.

Still ungradable (D22). With page access nothing changes: 'aggressive' expansion across the provider spectrum and partnering instability have no public series. Individual events (IBM Granite open release, Databricks-Tabular) are anecdotes, not a measure. Earlier adjudication stands.

Still ungradable (D23). No public measure of the share of service engagements with GenAI-enabled delivery. Services firms disclose GenAI bookings or revenue (e.g. Accenture), a share of value, not of engagements: a proxy. Looked for: IDC services trackers, provider disclosures counting engagements.

Still ungradable (D23). Opened the pages the earlier pass could not: Gartner's 2023 CIO survey (n=2,457) reports 70% call GenAI game-changing, 9% deployed, 55% plan to within 24 months: attitude and plans, not pressure. Salesforce/Vanson Bourne (600 IT professionals, Dec 2023-Jan 2024) says GenAI is the #1 technology IT feels pressure to onboard quickly and 88% cannot keep up with AI requests, but gives no share of CIOs feeling pressure. RWS reports 87% of C-suite executives feel pressure, a different population. EY 2024 US CIO sentiment survey has no pressure share. No measure of this population and behaviour.

Still ungradable (D23). Public CIO surveys rank data and analytics among top investment areas (Gartner 2023 release: cybersecurity, data analytics, cloud) but give no share of CIOs prioritising strategic data management with a comparable definition. Ranking is not the share.

Still ungradable (D22/D23). No public survey measures attainment of CIOs' 2025 digital revenue goals. Gartner's 2023 survey reports share of digital initiatives meeting outcome targets (43% operator, 63% franchiser), a different quantity and year.

Session rule: a share of CIOs is gradable against a survey of the same population and behaviour at the target year or the year before. The 2025 Gartner CIO and Technology Executive Survey (3,186 CIOs and technology executives, 88 countries, fielded 2024, published October 2024) reports 37% of organizations had already deployed GenAI. Error |35-37|/37 = 5.4%: hit under D16 numeric. Grader A's factor-of-2 range mixes populations and years: the Gartner Q4 2023 survey (29%) and McKinsey State of AI (about 65%) are not CIO surveys, and the 2024 CIO survey (9% deployed) was fielded in 2023 and is superseded by the target-year survey of the same population. With same-population data only, D23's range test does not trigger. Uncertainty: the 37% figure was confirmed via search results only (Gartner pages return 403 to fetch); a broader reading of 'embrace' (deployed or piloting) is not measured by any CIO survey and would not lower the verdict below partial.

Still ungradable (D22/D23). No public 2024-2025 CIO survey gives a share motivated or planning to automate compliance and ESG reporting. Looked for: Gartner, Foundry, IDC CIO surveys on compliance/ESG automation.

Still ungradable (D22/D23). No public survey of the G1000 (or the largest firms) measures difficulty with divergent regulation in 2025. Looked for: IDC, Gartner, KPMG/EY large-enterprise regulatory surveys giving this share. Note: earlier graders cite US51736824, the IT Industry 2025 edition; the claim is from the CIO Agenda 2025 FutureScape.

Surveys of organizations measuring this behaviour exist for 2024 and 2025, so grader A's 'no such survey found' is a search gap. Estimates on the dominant reading (in place or in progress): IAPP, spring 2024, 77% working on AI governance; Pacific AI, Feb-May 2025, 75% have AI usage policies; PEX Report 2025/26, 43% have an AI governance policy plus 25% implementing one = 68%. Range 68-77%, within a factor of 2 (D23). Median 75%; |85-75|/75 = 13.3%: partial. Grader B's median of two (76%, 11.8%) gives the same verdict. Narrower readings (formal governance framework 36%, dedicated role 59%, risk-evaluation process 45%) would be a miss, but 'be formalizing' is progressive and names policies first, so the broad reading dominates. Sample caveat: all three are self-selected professional surveys, not representative panels.

Still ungradable (D23). Found IDC's 2023/2024 CIO Sentiment Survey via CIO.com: nearly 4 in 10 CIOs expected to overspend on digital infrastructure and 47% of those blamed tech debt; CIOs ranked tech debt elimination well below AI and security. Neither is the share of CIOs driving enterprise remediation initiatives, and it predates the target year. Gartner's '<20% of software leaders are very effective at managing tech debt' is another construct. No measure of the claim's quantity. Note: earlier graders cite US51736824, the IT Industry 2025 edition; the claim is from the CIO Agenda 2025 FutureScape.

Both graders agree on the fact: Google Translate's Android Conversation Mode launched January 2011 (English-Spanish; 14 languages by October 2011). D16 grades hit if true by target_year + 2; January 2011 is well inside the 2010+2 window, and the rule does not penalise arrival within two years. Grader B applied a late-arrival penalty that D16 does not impose inside the +2 window. Hit.

The sentence follows the body-LAN sentence and says 'these truly personal computers', so the referent is the small carried devices, not notebooks. In 2009 phones and smartphones used flash memory only, and most music players were flash (nano, shuffle, touch). This meets the device test (more than 50% of new units). Notebooks still used hard disks, but the text does not refer to them. Grader B's notebook reading is less faithful to the antecedent.

Grader B says no such device existed by 2009. That is wrong. Benenson and Shapiro demonstrated a programmable autonomous molecular computer in 2001 and in 2004 an autonomous DNA automaton that evaluated cancer-gene expression and on its own released an antisense drug molecule. Autonomous DNA walkers were shown in 2003-2004. Nanoengineering was not a practical technology in 2009. Both halves hold. The devices are molecular, not Drexler-style atom-by-atom assemblers; the text's 'molecule by molecule' covers them.

Routine-use test: more than 20% of the relevant industry. In 2009, 94% of US public school teachers used grading systems, 96% word processing and 94% the internet for instruction or administration; 97% of schools had classroom computers. 'All facets' is an overstatement, but routine use far above the 20% threshold across teaching and administration meets the rule. B's 'computer-centred instruction' test adds a condition the text does not state.

Both trends were real by 2009. World printing and writing paper production peaked in 2007 at about 120 Mt and fell in 2008-2009, and has not regained the peak. Google had scanned about 7 million books by November 2008 and 12 million by June 2010. Grader A tested completion (share of all titles scanned), but the text claims a rate, not completion.

In 2009 the share was near zero, so no hit and no 'measurable by 2009' partial. The question is the 3-5 year window. Sub-pound high-resolution tablets arrived in 2012-2013 (iPad mini 0.68 lb, Nexus 7, Kindle Fire HD). Pearson's 2013 survey found about three in ten US students in grades 4-12 owned a tablet, with younger students more likely; 42% of high-school students used tablets regularly in 2014. A large part of the tablets children owned were 7-8 inch models under a pound. This puts ownership of a matching device near the 20% line in 2013-2014. Grader A's claim of under 5% by 2014 is not supported. Low certainty: no source splits student tablet ownership by weight.

The text says materials 'are accessed through wireless communication'; it does not say 'mainly'. Routine-use test (20% of the relevant industry): in fall 2008, 39% of US public schools had whole-school wireless and 30% partial wireless, 58% had laptop carts, and 94% of teachers used the internet for instruction or administration. Wireless access to learning materials was routine in well over 20% of schools. B's 'mainly wireless' test adds a word the text does not contain.

The claim has three parts. Part 1 (teacher-led instruction still prevalent) is true. Part 2 (increasing reliance on software approaches) has a measurable share: 55% of US school districts had students in distance-education courses in 2009-10, with about 1.8 million enrollments, and cognitive tutors ran in thousands of schools. Part 3 (teachers attend primarily to motivation and well-being) did not happen by 2014. A measurable share above 5% but below mainstream by 2009 fits partial. A's miss grades only part 3.

Acceptance is measurable where the systems were used. Print-to-speech software (Kurzweil 3000 and similar) was used and accepted among students with learning disabilities. The LeapFrog Tag, a pen that reads printed children's books aloud, sold more than 2 million readers in 2008-2009, a share above 5% of US children of the target age. General routine use by most children (claim 040) did not happen. Measurable, below mainstream, gives partial. A's miss rests on 'under 5%' without a source and ignores consumer read-aloud devices.

The only measured quantity is formal learning time: about 32 hours per employee per year around 2009-2011, about 1.6% of a 2,000-hour year, and flat, not growing. No source shows learning as a significant share of work time in most jobs, by 2009 or by 2014. B's test (share of workers who get some training) measures a different claim (see 047). Informal learning is not measured, so it cannot support a hit or partial.

Routine-use test (20% of the relevant population). In 2004-05, 27% of US adults took work-related courses in one year, the most common adult-education activity. Employers delivered about 32 formal learning hours per employee every year, and many licensed professions required continuing education. Recurring training reached well over 20% of workers. 'Most careers' is not directly measured, but the rule's mainstream threshold is met.

The verb is 'have been introduced'. Talking GPS devices for blind travellers were on sale: Trekker (reviewed 2003), BrailleNote GPS, and Trekker Breeze ($895, reviewed March 2009), which announced streets and intersections and guided users back to route. In the sentence, GPS attaches most naturally to 'finding their way around'; separate electronic obstacle aids also existed. GPS did not detect obstacles, which is a weakness in wording, not a failure of the main claim.

No real-time speech translation was in common use in 2009, so the share was under 5% at the placed year. Google Translate added speech input in 2010 and an experimental English-Spanish conversation mode in January 2011; use stayed far below 20% through 2014. Neither partial condition holds: no 5% share by 2009, and no mainstream use in 2012-2014. B's partial rests on 'likely above 5% of smartphone users trying it', which is not a D16 condition.

User test (20% of target users in major markets). By April 2009, 56% of US adults had gone online wirelessly (Wi-Fi or mobile), and Kindle and iPhone delivered books, music and apps over the air. A used mobile broadband subscriptions worldwide (13%), which excludes Wi-Fi and averages in non-major markets. 'Ever-present, high-bandwidth' overstates 2009 coverage, but wireless delivery was mainstream in major markets.

The book itself places this as a non-mainstream practice, so the mainstream test does not apply; the test is presence at a measurable level. Remote sexual activity was practised in 2009: webcam sex, cybersex, and avatar sex in Second Life adult regions (peak 88,200 concurrent users in 2009). In 2012, 6% of US adult cell owners had sent and 15% had received a sext. A's VR-mainstream reading contradicts the author's own next sentence.

Popular means mainstream here. No source shows virtual-partner use at 5% or more of adults in major markets by 2009 or by 2014. LovePlus (Japan only, September 2009) and adult areas of Second Life were niches. Both graders agree use was niche; B gives partial without a 5% figure, and D16 partial needs a measurable share of at least 5%.

The observable part has a dominant reading and data: a 2007 Duke/Berkeley study found a foreign-born key founder in 25.3% of US engineering and technology companies founded 1995-2005, with $52bn in 2005 sales. The 'ideal heritage' explanation is opinion and cannot be tested, but an untestable explanation does not give a different verdict; no faithful reading of the text gives a miss. D16 allows unfalsifiable only when readings give different verdicts.

Mixed. OECD 2009 data name Israel, Sweden, Switzerland, the UK and the US as the developed venture-capital markets; Japan is not among them and only 2% of Japanese start-ups got VC, so Europe ahead of Japan holds. Korea is a counterexample: OECD ranks it among the leading countries in VC as a share of GDP. Venture capital stayed under 0.05% of GDP in most countries in 2009, so 'popular throughout the world' is only partly true, though VC and employee share schemes existed in many countries. One comparison holds, one fails: partial.

Mainstream test (20% of target users). By 2009 the iTunes Store was the largest US music vendor (from April 2008), had previews and secure checkout, and was on iPhone over Wi-Fi and 3G from 2007; the App Store passed 1 billion downloads in April 2009. Download over home Wi-Fi to laptops was common (56% of US adults online wirelessly in 2009). A's own test, 35% smartphone ownership in May 2011, is within 2 years and above 20%, which D16 grades as a hit.

Computerworld (28 Aug 2000) gives about 60 embedded processors per US household, and Turley (2002, found by search) gives 40-50; no source measures the 2009 figure. Both graders chose partial without an actual value, so the D16 quantitative band cannot be applied.

The sentence depends on claim 101 (a growing neo-Luddite movement), which did not appear in measurable form. The predicate 'influence is limited' is true; the presupposed movement and the causal mechanism fail or cannot be tested. Neither reading is more faithful to the text: the sentence asserts the limit and presupposes the movement equally. The readings give hit and miss. D16 gives unfalsifiable.

FRED/Census SAIPE confirms poverty 11.9% (1999) and 14.3% (2009); a 'stable' forecast of 11.9% is 16.8% off the actual 14.3%, and the count (32.8M vs 43.6M) is 24.8% off, so both measures fall inside the D16 25% band. Grader B's statement that both exceed 25% is an arithmetic error; 'continuing concern' held.

The observable state held: the poor did not form a significant political movement in 2009-2011, and public assistance expanded (ARRA raised SNAP benefits from April 2009; participation peaked at 47.6 million in 2013). The 2009 recession raised poverty to 14.3%, but US income per head stayed among the highest in the world, so 'generally high level of affluence' is weakened, not false. Occupy (2011) was not an underclass movement. The mechanism cannot be tested, but no faithful reading gives a miss on the observable state. Low-to-medium certainty.

Auto-accompaniment was in wide amateur use: arranger keyboards follow the chords a player enters live and generate a backing band, and Band-in-a-Box (since 1990) generates backing and solos. That is a basic 'cybernetic musician' that responds to the player's chords, and its use by amateur keyboard players is a measurable share. Responsive improvising partners stayed in research labs, so 'routinely jam' with responsive musicians was not mainstream by 2014. Measurable but below mainstream gives partial. No usage statistics exist, so certainty is low.

The software existed by 2009: Band-in-a-Box, GarageBand with Magic GarageBand (bundled with every Mac), and Microsoft Songsmith (early 2009), which generates accompaniment for a sung melody. Under D16 the claim reads as mainstream use, and no source shows 20% of non-musician music lovers creating music with such software by 2011. Products on sale and bundled at scale, with thousands of shared user songs, show measurable use below mainstream. B's availability reading ignores the D16 frame.

Machine translation was in mass use by 2009-2011: Google Translate (2006; about 23 languages by January 2009), Babel Fish, Bing Translator and Chrome's built-in page translation (2010). Google Translate served over 200 million people a day by May 2013. Casual use by internet users reading foreign-language text meets the mainstream test. B's narrower reading (publication-grade translation of books) adds a restriction the text does not state. Medium certainty: no retrieved figure for 2009-2011 exactly.

In the book's 2009 chapter, virtual environments are screen and eyeglass based (claims 010, 017, 073); immersive direct-eye VR is placed in the 2019 chapter. So the dominant 2009 reading is interactive environments as software, which covers games and simulations. In 2008, 53% of US adults and 97% of teens played video games, and World of Warcraft had over 10 million subscribers. That clears the 20% mainstream test. The rafting and movie-star examples are illustrative; the movie-star example did not occur.

The sentence is mainly a statement of limit, and the limit held: consumer haptics in 2009 were controller rumble and force-feedback wheels and joysticks. The audiovisual part holds under the same reading as claim 123: 3D game environments with surround sound were a mass entertainment form in 2009. A graded 'compelling VR' as consumer head-mounted VR, which the book places in 2019, not 2009.

Wikipedia confirms Cyber Command was ordered 23 Jun 2009 as a sub-unified command and elevated only in 2017; GAO-11-695R puts DoD cybersecurity budget estimates at $2.3-3.2B for FY2012, under 1% of the DoD budget. The claimed 'primary focus' did not occur by 2014, and no D16 branch gives partial.

Dominance was not reached: in 2009 the wars were fought mainly by about 186,000 US ground troops and manned aircraft, and drones were remotely piloted, not autonomous. But unmanned aircraft had a large measurable share: DoD inventory grew from 167 in 2002 to nearly 7,500 in 2010, and the unmanned share of DoD aircraft rose from 5% in 2005 to about 41% by 2010-2012. A measurable share well above 5% but short of dominance by the placed year gives partial.

Computerised records were mainstream among office physicians by 2011 (57% any EMR, 34% basic), so the loose reading is a hit. But the text says lifetime records. Longitudinal lifetime records existed only in integrated systems (VA, Kaiser) and some small national systems; records elsewhere stayed fragmented across providers through 2014. A measurable share (more than 5% of US patients in VA and Kaiser alone is near the line) below mainstream gives partial. B's reading drops the word that makes the claim a forecast.

Attention rose around 2008-2009. Springer published 'Parsing the Turing Test' (January 2008), a 518-page multi-author volume with a Dennett foreword. The 2008 Loebner Prize at the University of Reading, where programs fooled 3 of 12 judges, drew wide press coverage. The 2012 centenary was larger, but 'renewed interest' needs a visible rise, not a peak, and the rise is dated 2008. Medium certainty: no attention index was retrieved.

The first clause (computers still fail) is true. The forecast is the trend in confidence, and the text does not say whose. The only survey (AGI-09, self-selected optimists) supports reading 1; mainstream AI opinion of the period was more sceptical, and the 2002 Kapor-Kurzweil bet framed the question as open. No series measures a change in confidence between 1999 and 2009. Neither reading dominates, the readings point to different verdicts, and the trend itself has no measure.

Compound claim. The communication half held strongly (93% of world population within 3G+ reach, 95% mobile-broadband coverage by 2021; 4G speeds orders above 1999 dial-up). The 'computing embedded everywhere' half (ubiquitous computing in objects) was only partly realised by 2021 (see the separate 148 claim). One half mainstream, one half below it = partly true. Partial.

Grader A called it ungradable for want of a direct workload-share series, but the claim is a 'majority' (>50%) threshold that bounding evidence clearly falsifies: in 2019-2024 the overwhelming bulk of executed compute ran conventional software (OS, web, databases, business apps), AI-accelerated servers were a minority even of data-centre growth, and genetic algorithms are marginal. A threshold this far from met does not need a precise series to be graded, so D22 ungradable does not apply. Miss.

The sentence predicts two modes: reading on hand-held screens and, as the more common mode, direct-eye displays. Hand-held reading became routine and mainstream (phones, tablets, e-readers carried the majority of reading). The 'more commonly direct-eye' mode failed (AR/retinal eyewear stayed niche). One named mode held at mainstream, the dominant mode failed = partly true. Grader A graded only the failed direct-eye mode; the hand-held clause is part of the forecast and held. Partial.

The claim's wording is 'very effective and widely used', not 'used by a majority of candidates'. Both parts held: implants are the established, highly effective standard of care for severe-to-profound deafness, with ~736,900 registered worldwide by December 2019 (over 1 million by 2022) and routine deployment across all major markets, including the majority of eligible children in developed countries. Grader B's 20%-of-all-candidates test reads in a penetration threshold the claim does not state. Hit.

The verb is 'have emerged' - an existence/appearance claim, not a mainstream-adoption claim. Commercial glasses-free 'holographic' light-field displays existed by 2018 (Looking Glass shipped December 2018), satisfying emergence. Grader B graded down because true diffraction holograms remained prototypes, but that imposes a stricter definition than the label's 'emerged'. The dominant reading of the claim is met. Hit.

Under the decade-chapter rule (hit if true by target_year + 2 = 2021), the claim held: by 2020-2021 meetings moved online at scale (Zoom to >300 million daily participants April 2020; 67% of US white-collar workers remote in part by September 2021), so most meetings did not require physical proximity. The rule grades the outcome inside the window; the pandemic cause and the later partial reversal do not disqualify a within-window hit. Grader A's requirement of a durable majority of all meetings is stricter than D16's window test. Hit.

Two components. The 'all done through the ever-present web' component held near-universally (streaming, web-delivered media and calls were ubiquitous by 2019). The 'via worn/direct-eye devices' delivery mechanism failed (media ran on phones/PCs/TVs; AR/VR headsets 11.2M shipments in 2021, far below any share threshold; 3D calls niche). One component true at mainstream, the specific delivery mechanism below 5% = partly true. Grader A graded only the worn-device mechanism; the web-delivery of these activities is real and massive. Partial.

The claim is modest ('superior in SOME ways, such as...') and names two specific advantages: very reliable memory and programmable personalities. Both held by 2019-2021: assistants and companion apps (Replika, voice assistants used by ~1 billion people) had exact recall of stored data and configurable, scripted personas. Grader A graded down on conversational-memory limits, but the claim's 'very reliable memories' points to stored-data recall, which digital systems trivially have. The stated narrow superiorities held. Hit.

First clause held throughout 2019-2021 (chatbots widely seen as far less subtle than humans). The second clause only requires that 'there is disagreement', a low bar met by 2019-2021: companion-app users (Replika) treated bots as partners, a visible minority dissent, later sharpened by the June 2022 LaMDA episode. Grader A set the bar at a prominent public controversy and so dated it to 2022; the claim's wording ('there is disagreement') was already satisfied within the 2019+2 window. Hit.

The dominant reading of 'sufficient prosperity to provide' is a capacity claim, not a claim that necessities are universally provided, so this is not a case of two equally faithful readings diverging - D16 unfalsifiable does not apply, and Grader B's call is set aside. Under the dominant (capacity) reading: the controversies-persist clause held (welfare/responsibility debates continued), and aggregate world output could cover basic necessities at modest cost; but necessities were in fact not secured for ~700 million people in extreme poverty, so the implied state of affairs was only partly realised. Partly true. Partial.

The claim states a specific quantity: the share of working time (across most jobs) spent on the employee's own learning, and that it is growing. No public series measures this. Grader A graded partial off adult-learning participation rates (share of adults who take any training), which is a different quantity - a proxy, not a measure of the stated share of work time. Under D23 a proxy of another quantity is not a measure. Ungradable (looked for: share of working time spent learning across employment; ATD State-of-the-Industry hours-per-employee and OECD/Eurostat adult-learning participation measure neither the share of work time nor its trend).

By 2018-2019 AI artists were emerging and taken seriously in visual art (Edmond de Belamy sold at Christie's for $432,500, 2018) and music (AIVA recognised by SACEM, 2016), but critics largely treated these as novelty, and 'all of the arts' (literature and others) lagged. Wide serious engagement across the arts arrived with the 2022-2024 generative-AI wave (within the 3-5-year window). The claim's qualifiers ('all', 'taken seriously') were only partly met by 2021. Grader A's hit undervalues those qualifiers. Partial.

Cited sources (Wikipedia 'Midjourney', 'Theatre D'opera Spatial', 'AIVA') are anecdotes with no share of working artists using AI, in 2019 or 2022-2024, so neither the >=5% nor the mainstream-in-3-5-years branch is shown. Readings also split: machine-intelligence features in standard tools (auto-tune, content-aware fill) were typical in 2019, which would read as hit.

Video games clearly surpassed film and recorded music by revenue (US games matched US film at ~$43bn in 2018; global games ~$179bn 2020, ~$191bn 2021, roughly double film). But the claim is 'the type ... in greatest demand ... continues to be', i.e. the single largest over all entertainment, and television/video (pay-TV plus advertising plus streaming) remains a larger aggregate that neither grader shows smaller. Games is the largest discrete interactive product but not clearly the single greatest entertainment product overall. Partly true. Partial.

World Bank SP.DYN.LE00.IN 2019 vs 100 years (D16 numeric, error relative to actual): World 72.9 (37%, miss), US 78.8 (27%, miss), but EU 81.3 (23%), OECD 80.2 (24.6%), high income 80.2 (24.7%) and Japan 84.4 (18.5%) are within 25%, i.e. partial. The industrial-revolution frame points to developed countries, which sit at the partial/miss boundary; A misapplied the band (miss at 15%) and B wrongly said the developed-country reading is a miss.

The 2017 horsepox synthesis (~$100,000, mail-order DNA, a funded university team) shows the capability had descended to a modestly resourced lab and drew expert alarm - but it required ~$100k, specialised tacit skill and controls, which is above the claim's specific 'typical graduate student' threshold. Grader A equates 'academic lab/team' with 'typical graduate student'; the claim names the latter. Capability trending toward but not yet at the stated level = partly true. Partial.

The claim has checkable components, so D22 ungradable (Grader B) does not apply. The 'major focus of international security agencies' component is falsifiable and largely failed pre-COVID (the 2018 US National Defense Strategy centred on great-power competition, not biothreats); bioengineered countermeasures did advance (mRNA design in days; first authorisation Dec 2020) but were not recognised as a 'comparable' offset and biosecurity was not the agencies' major focus in 2019. Part true, part false. Partial.

The 'do not meet expert criteria' clause held strongly (Eugene Goostman's 2014 'pass' widely rejected by experts). But the 'prevalent reports' clause was not met by 2019: Turing-pass reports were occasional (Goostman and a few chatbot claims), not prevalent, until the generative-AI wave of 2022-2023, 3-4 years after target (within the 3-5-year window). Grader A's hit understates 'prevalent'. Partly true. Partial.

The consensus clause ('not yet passed') held firmly through 2019-2021. The 'growing controversy' clause, read as a genuine live dispute over whether machines had passed a valid test, materialised with large language models in 2022-2024 (LaMDA sentience claim June 2022; 'ChatGPT broke the Turing test' 2023; GPT-4/GPT-4.5 pass studies 2024-2025), 3-5 years after target. In 2019-2021 the matter was relatively settled among experts. Partly true (consensus held; the growing controversy came in the 3-5-year window). Partial.

The dominant reading - devices tapping vast remote compute and memory over high-speed links - was realised by 2010-2012 via cloud computing (AWS 2006, Azure 2010) plus mobile broadband, with mobile apps routinely offloading to the cloud. The parenthetical 'mesh' (every device becoming a web server in a peer supercomputer) is Kurzweil's gloss on the architecture and did not form, but the substantive claim held. Grader B weights the failed peer-mesh detail over the realised substance. Hit.

Always-on wireless Internet was arriving (3G smartphones gave constant connectivity, LTE launched Dec 2009), satisfying 'at all times'. But 'very high-bandwidth' is the load-bearing qualifier: around 2010-2012 most mobile data still ran on 3G (a few Mbps), and very-high-bandwidth 4G/LTE did not reach mainstream (~20% of users in major markets) until ~2013-2014 - mainstream 3-5 years after the placed year. Grader A counts the LTE launch but it was not widespread by 2012. Partly true. Partial.

Read in context (items 004-007 describe tiny displays projecting images, AR overlays and augmented perception), 'project auditory environments' means immersive/spatial soundscapes, not ordinary stereo earphones. Immersive spatial audio in tiny earbuds arrived ~2020 (AirPods Pro spatial audio), ten years late and beyond the 5-year window. The trivial 'personal audio' reading that Grader B uses treats the prediction as the already-mundane earphone, which is not the dominant contextual reading. Miss.

Around 2010 AR existed only as niche smartphone apps (Layar/Wikitude 2009, Word Lens Dec 2010), well below the D16 5% partial floor, and mass AR use (Pokemon Go) did not arrive until July 2016 - six years later, outside the 3-5-year mainstream window. Neither D16 partial condition is met (no >=5% share by 2010-2012; mainstream not reached within 3-5 years). Grader B granted partial on the mere existence of AR apps without a 5% share. Miss.

The claim's mechanism is brain scanning contributing to the model. By 2025-2026 it has not: the effective AI systems of the period (LLMs/GPT-4) are trained on text, not derived from brain scans, and connectomics remains at fruit-fly / ~1 mm3-mouse scale with no scan-derived model of human intelligence. Grader A graded partial by crediting LLMs, but LLMs do not satisfy 'brain scanning contributes'. The stated route did not deliver; a reversal by 2027-2030 is not supported by current connectomics. Miss (window nominally open to 2030, but the brain-scanning mechanism shows no sign of delivering).

Quote and footnote confirmed (2022 PDF p.96) and Gartner (Jul 2025) security services 2025 = $83.8bn (+21%, partial), but Precedence Research puts 2025 cybersecurity services (professional incl. integration, support, consulting + managed) at $177.3bn (-43%, miss); estimates of the same quantity span >2x, so under D23 the claim is ungradable, not partial. Graders used one estimate only.

Third-party question (D30): the edition (p. text checked in the archived PDF) states the figure in McKinsey's own voice ('are expected to open by 2025') with no footnote or attribution; the match to DOE's Dec-2021 list of 13 new gigafactories is grader A's inference, and the edition's frame (13 of ~30, incl. already-operational plants) is not the DOE frame (13 new plants). So it is the publisher's forecast, not a quoted figure. Measure (D23): the Dallas Fed (2026-03-03) counts the same quantity for the same scope - US battery gigafactories of the recent build-out: 12 operating and 23 under construction (35 total, consistent with the edition's ~30 frame). Different vintage/method of the same quantity is gradable under D23; only one public tally found, so no range test applies. Grader A's 'no public tally found' is superseded by this source, which grader B cited. Arithmetic: 13 forecast vs 12 actual, error 1/12 = 8.3% (B's '+8%' is correct) -> within 10% -> hit. Grader B's alternative DOE-list reading (miss) is less faithful because the edition does not cite or reproduce that list. Uncertainty: the Dallas Fed count is dated March 2026 rather than 31 Dec 2025 and does not state whether pre-2021 plants (e.g. Panasonic Nevada, AESC Smyrna, LGES Holland) are included; if they were added the operating count would be ~15 and the verdict would drop to partial (13 vs 15 = 13%).

Test: 20% of target users, measured as China's mobile-payment users who pay by face. Both graders cite about 118 million face-payment users in 2019 against more than 700 million mobile-payment users, about 17%: below 20% at placed year + 2, so not a hit. That share is well above 5% inside the window, so the verdict is partial whether the later figure (about 495 million in 2021, mainstream 4 years after) holds or not. Grader A reached hit by adding iPhone Face ID to Chinese face payment; that sums two different populations and measures, and A itself notes face payment alone was under 20%. Face ID hardware on new iPhones is not 50% of new smartphones, so the device-feature test does not rescue a hit either. The 120 million in the article are Alipay users, not face-payment users.

FDA list confirms Luxturna, Zolgensma, Hemgenix, Elevidys, Casgevy (59 products listed, not 66). The hit rests on an approval event test that D16 does not provide; no grader shows 20% (or even 5%) of patients with targeted inherited disorders treated, and uptake of several (e.g. hemophilia) gene therapies is known to be low.

Test: routine use by 20% of the relevant industry (manufacturers of metal parts), 5% floor. Every survey found samples firms that already use additive manufacturing (Stratasys Direct 2019, AMFG 2019 '49% of companies use metal AM', Jabil 2019 '40% use 3-D printing for production'), not manufacturers at large, and none gives metal AM in routine production as a share of manufacturers. Grader B's partial asserts a share above 5% and below 20% without a measure of either bound: its cited 12% and 49% are shares of AM users, a different population. Market-size figures (AMPOWER) are a different quantity. No public measure exists for the stated quantity (D22).

The claim names embryo-like structures, which existed at publication (Cambridge 2017-18). Within placed year + 2 several labs published stem-cell embryo models: mouse gastruloids (Beccari et al., Nature, Oct 2018), trunk-like structures (Veenvliet et al., Science, 2020), and human gastruloids (Moris et al., Nature, June 2020). That is routine research use, mouse and human, by 2020: hit. Grader B raised the bar to 'complete' embryo models (2022 mouse, 2023 human), which the claim does not state; that is a reading error. Grader A's hit is right but its evidence (2022, 2023) falls outside the hit window. No share-of-labs measure exists; the call rests on the shared lab-method test both graders used.

Test: 20% of earbud users using in-ear live translation (5% floor), or 50% of new earbuds shipping with it. No public figure exists for Pixel Buds sales, for use of Google's interpreter through earbuds, or for the share of earbuds supporting it. Google extended the feature to all Assistant-optimised headphones in 2018, and phone-side conversation mode works with any earbuds, so feature support cannot be bounded by vendor share either. Grader B's 'below 5% through 2023' is inferred from the absence of adoption data and from Apple (2025) and Samsung (2024) adding the feature late; that dates the arrival of the feature at two vendors, not the share of users. Ungradable (D22): looked for Pixel Buds sales, Translate conversation-mode usage, surveys of earbud translation use.

Test: 20% of adults in major markets receiving a genome-based polygenic risk prediction; 5% floor within 2018-2023. Clinical PRS stayed in research trials (not standard of care as of 2021). The consumer channel: 23andMe first issued polygenic reports in 2019. Grader A's 'roughly 5% at most' divides 23andMe's 14 million customers (Feb 2024, outside the window, worldwide, and including ancestry-only customers) by US adults; that is an upper bound of a larger population, not the measured share. Health-report customers within the window are a smaller subset, and against adults in all major markets the share is far below 5%. Miss; window closed 2023.

Test: routine use by 20% of the relevant industry (warehouse and fulfilment operations using learned robotic piece picking); partial needs 5% by 2024. Interact Analysis counts just over 3,000 picking robots shipped worldwide in 2024 outside Amazon; a cumulative fleet of that order cannot reach 5% of the world's warehouses. Amazon's arms (Sparrow, Robin, Vulcan) are one operator with no disclosed share of picks. Grader A's ungradable is defensible for a precise share, but the shipment count bounds the share well below 5%, which is enough for a miss. Provisional miss, window closes 2029. Note: the Interact Analysis page was blocked (captcha) on re-fetch; the figure is taken from Grader B's search summary.

Test: 20% of target users (consumers in launch markets) paying with the new digital currency; 5% floor within 2020-2025. Libra/Diem never launched and was sold in 2022. e-CNY counted 261 million wallets by end-2021, but wallets were opened in a trial pushed with more than RMB 150 million of giveaways, and total transactions were US$13.8 billion, about US$53 per wallet over the trial; WeChat Pay and Alipay kept more than 90% of electronic payments. A wallet opened is not use of the money. Grader A graded wallet counts as users; that measures accounts, not payment. No public figure shows 5% of consumers paying with e-CNY. Miss, window closed 2025. Least certain: on wallet counts the verdict would be partial.

The entry says scientists have already used AI to discover drug-like compounds, and its 'why it matters' names the difficulty of finding promising molecules as the cost driver. What becomes available in 3-5 years is therefore the discovery method in practice, not a share of approved drugs; Grader A's reading (b), share of clinical candidates, is less faithful to the text, so the dominant reading is graded (D16) and unfalsifiable does not apply. Test: routine use by 20% of the industry. ICON/GlobalData found 49% of pharma and biotech R&D professionals using AI/Big Data in R&D in 2024 (39% in 2019); 16 of the top 20 pharmas' executives call AI an immediate priority; AI-discovered candidates are in phase 2 and 3 trials. Mainstream by 2027: hit. Note the surveys sample professionals and executives, not firms.

Test: 20% of target users, i.e. households and sites lacking terrestrial broadband, with the US as the measured major market. Starlink had about 1 million subscribers worldwide in Dec 2022 and about 1.4 million in the US by Aug 2024, against about 7 to 7.5 million unserved US locations in 2024 (about 19%); 2.7 million US subscribers by mid-2026. Mainstream arrives around 2025, 5 years after the placed year, and the share passed 5% by about 2022: partial either way. Grader B measured share of the satellite-broadband market (already a small niche of users), which tests whether Starlink beat GEO providers, not adoption by target users; B itself notes the household reading gives a lower verdict. Not every Starlink subscriber sits at an unserved location, which makes this an upper bound and does not lift it to a hit.

Both graders agree on the facts: US adults who had used ChatGPT were 18% in July 2023 (Pew), below 20%, and 34% by Feb-Mar 2025. The dispute is the base. The entry's own framing is a developer platform (API, apps built on it, code generation), so routine use by the relevant industry is the dominant D16 test. Stack Overflow 2023 (survey May 2023): 44% of respondents already use AI tools in their development process (26% more plan to), and 83% of AI-search users used ChatGPT, 55% of AI-dev-tool users Copilot (both GPT-family). That is above 20% of the industry within the +2 window: hit. Grader B cited the 70% 'use or plan to use' figure; the currently-using figure (44%, Stack Overflow blog) is the right one and still clears the bar. Grader A's general-public base is a valid secondary test and is borderline rather than clearly late (Pew's next reading, Feb 2024, was 23%), so it does not dominate.

Only evidence is one Wikipedia sentence that synthetic data 'has become a core component of the post-training pipeline' for LLMs, with no adoption figures; that is a practice of a few frontier labs, not a measured 20% of organisations training AI, and the claim's framing (privacy- and bias-safe data sold by vendors) is untested. Too weak for hit or any other verdict.

Grader B is right that no survey gives the share of archaeology projects using ancient DNA (one search for a bibliometric share found none). But D22 applies when no public measure of what the claim states exists, and this claim states a capability in routine use, which is measured: the Allen Ancient DNA Resource records about 10 individuals per year with genome-wide data in 2010-2014, about 200 per year in 2015-2017 and thousands per year since 2018, passing 10,000 by end-2022; the entry itself gives 5 (2010) to 5,550 (2020) whole-genome individuals. In the relevant field, studies of ancient human population history, genome-wide aDNA is the standard method at the placed year, the same routine-use-in-its-community test the consensus applied to JWST and Rubin. Hit; least certain call, as the share of the wider archaeology field is unmeasured.

Device reading checks out (Counterpoint: GenAI phones ~1/3 of 2025 shipments; IDC: 18% in 2024), giving partial. But the entry names cloud small models (GPT-4o mini, Claude Haiku) as much as on-device ones, and Wikipedia 'GPT-4o' shows GPT-4o mini replaced GPT-3.5 Turbo as ChatGPT's free-tier model in July 2024, which on a usage reading would put a small model in front of >20% of US adults (Pew 34%) and give hit. Two faithful readings, different verdicts; neither grader tested the cloud one.

D30 state of affairs over 1997-2010. The source context defines weakness as a lack of economic resources for great-power status, not as stagnation. Held in part: 1998 default and collapse (GDP $196 bn in 1999), 2009 contraction of 7.8%, and in 2010 Russia was about 2.3% of world GDP, about a tenth of the US, and still commodity-dependent. Failed in part: 1999-2008 growth of 5-10% a year, dollar GDP up from $405 bn to $1.66 tn, large reserves, debt repaid, and enough resources to fund military revival (Georgia 2008). Grader B graded a growth/stagnation reading that is narrower than the source's capability framing; B's 'high-income on 2012 data' falls outside the target. No arithmetic errors found.

OWID/UN WPP 2024 population CSV: world +1,298.8 m 2000-2015, UN more developed regions (Europe, Northern America, Japan, Australia, NZ) +71.6 m, so the developing share is 94.49%, 0.51 pp from 95%: outside the D18 0.5 pp hit band, inside 1.0 pp. The World Bank income-group reading (about 91%) is further off. Graders rounded to 0.5.

A percent change is a level forecast (implied level 1.5x base), graded under the D16 numeric rule, not D18 points. Energy Institute via OWID: 105,981 TWh (2000) to 145,500 TWh (2015), ratio 1.373; forecast 1.5 is 9.3% above actual (hit). IEA TES as cited by B gives about 1.36 (10.3%, partial); D23 median of the two is about 1.366, 9.8% off: hit, but close to the edge. If the NIC's unstated base were 1997 rather than 2000, actual growth is larger and the hit is firmer. Sufficiency held: no lasting physical shortage through 2015. Grader A applied D18 percentage points to a level change (rule error); A's '8.5% under' also measures error against the forecast rather than the actual (D16 measures against the actual: 9.3%), though both are inside 10%. The IEA figure is B's and was not re-fetched.

D16 numeric level rule; measure not stated, so under D23 the market-rate and PPP real series are treated as estimates of the same quantity by different methods and graded on their median. GDP: 1.711 (market) and 1.876 (PPP), median 1.79 vs 1.80: hit. Per capita: 1.342 (market) and 1.472 (PPP), median 1.407; 1.5 is 6.6% above: hit. On market rates alone per capita is 11.8% off (partial), which is why B scored partial: B's arithmetic is correct, but B used one method where D23 requires the median. A's '6% off' for per capita is computed against the forecast; against the actual median it is 6.6%, still a hit. 2020 is the COVID trough; with 2019 the forecast is closer still.

The source context settles the reading: the line is the likely impact of 'a global multipolar system is emerging' and of the rising power of nonstate actors, and it continues 'Power will be more dispersed... traditional Western alliances will weaken'. A literal institutional reading (UN membership persists) is not equally faithful, so unfalsifiable does not apply (D16, D20). Under the context reading, held in part by 2025: rival blocs (expanded BRICS), Russia-West war, sanctions regimes, US withdrawal from several international bodies and strain on Western alliances. But the state-based multilateral system still functions (193 UN members, UNSC and UNGA operating), so 'will no longer exist' did not hold in full.

'Lag behind' is read as a level comparison with the countries that 'will have become middle income powers'; the next sentence uses 'lag behind' in the same level sense (Latin America vs Asia). Brazil, Mexico, Argentina, Colombia and Peru are upper-middle, Chile and Uruguay high income. Venezuela's real GDP per capita fell 68% (2008-2024) and it is lower-middle; Bolivia is lower-middle, at about a third of the regional real GDP per capita (3,046 vs 8,872 in 2024), and in a currency and fuel crisis by 2023-25. Haiti's real GDP per capita fell from 1,357 to 1,155, with gangs controlling most of Port-au-Prince. Grader A graded Bolivia's growth rate against the regional trend (it grew faster, +28% vs +12%), a narrower reading than the text supports. Grader B's 'Haiti low income' is wrong: the World Bank classes Haiti lower-middle income; the 'poorer' part holds on real GDP per capita, not on income group.

The view is not only a value judgment: telework expansion and work spilling into non-work time are measured. Both moved in the stated direction but modestly: ATUS share doing some work at home on workdays rose 19% (2003) to 23% (2014), and Pew 2014 found 35% of online workers say technology increased their hours. A real but minority blurring, not a significant erosion; 'sharply alter family dynamics' has no measure and is not graded. Held in part. Grader A's ungradable discards the measurable half.

The statement has no geographic limit, so the global reading dominates. RAND (2014) counted Salafi-jihadist groups rising 58% (31 to 49) 2010-2013 with fighters more than doubling, and ISIS drew tens of thousands of foreign fighters largely via online propaganda by 2014-15. Grader B's SPLC count of US hate groups (784 in 2014) is a US formal-group measure; SPLC itself attributes the drop to migration online, which fits the 'networks flourish online' clause rather than refuting growth.

The forecast's payoff, and the reason the statement exists, is higher social trust; network growth is the stated mechanism. Trust fell: GSS 'most people can be trusted' about 34% in 2018-2024, below mid-2000s GSS levels, and 71% of Americans in 2019 said interpersonal trust had declined. The consequence failed, so the view misses. Grader B's baseline is a reading error: the 44-45% figure for 2006 is from Pew's own 2006 survey, not the GSS, so the 44%-to-34% drop compares two different surveys (direction still holds on GSS alone).

The statement's headline is further polarization; filtering is its mechanism. The majority's rejection held on filtering: only about 21% of Americans were consistent ideologues with insulated media diets in 2014. It failed on polarization: partisan antipathy more than doubled 1994-2014 and the most polarized were also the most filtered. Grader A's hit grades only the 'most people filter' clause and drops the polarization clause the respondents also rejected.

The defining content of the rejected scenario is dangers 'not recognized until it is impossible to reverse them', which has no public measure. Grader B graded a narrower proxy (autonomous weapons) that the text does not name; for the named activities, fully automated pipelines did exist by 2020 (algorithmic mass surveillance, automated trading and content filtering), so even the proxy does not clearly support a hit. Looked for incident databases; they record recognized harms only.

Text says 'the only one for a majority of the people across the world'. Primary held: 92% of 4.54B internet users connected via mobile and mobile broadband (75 per 100) far exceeded fixed (about 15 per 100). 'Only one for a majority of the world' did not: only about 51-58% of the world was online at all, and three-quarters of users 16-64 also used computers, so mobile-only users were well under half the world's population. Grader A's reading drops the 'only one' clause.

The boundary claim is measurable even though 'net positive' is not (not graded). In 2020, 71% of telework-capable US workers worked from home all or most of the time and 49% of new teleworkers had more freedom over hours, so boundaries blurred widely; but it was pandemic-forced, not willing, only 38% found work-life balance easier, and right-to-disconnect laws (France 2017 onward) show boundaries were being restored, not erased. Held in part. Same treatment as 2005-004.

A causal judgment about the internet's net effect on three things; no public measure isolates it. Indicators point both ways: NAEP reading scores declined from 2015 (against), while the volume of writing and open reference works such as Wikipedia grew (for 'rendering of knowledge'). Grader B graded only test-score literacy and dropped 'rendering of knowledge'; NAEP cannot attribute the decline to internet use. Looked for NAEP and literacy trend data.

Both graders agree no verdict is possible; the question is which non-verdict. D16 unfalsifiable requires readings that each give a verdict. Here neither the product reading nor the category reading can be scored, because no public record exists of what 2010's 'savviest innovators' anticipated, and 'often' has no count. That is D22 ungradable. Looked for: a record of 2010 innovator expectations against 2020 hit products.

Not only a value judgment: the scenario makes a specific factual claim ('they do not suffer notable cognitive shortcomings as they multitask'), and the research record by 2018 went against it: heavy media multitaskers perform worse in several cognitive domains (Ophir 2009; Uncapher and Wagner 2018 review), consistent with option B's 'distracted, do not retain'. The review calls causation inconclusive, but the claim concerns shortcomings, not their cause. 'Wired differently' and 'positive overall' are not graded. Low confidence.

An adoption claim under D16 plus a displacement state. Mobile payment reached a measurable share: 46% of US consumers made at least one mobile payment in the 12 months to Oct 2020 (38% in 2019). The displacement failed: cash, debit and credit still made about three-quarters of US payments (19%, 28%, 27%). Adoption grew well past 5% while the stated end-state did not arrive, which is a partial, not a miss. Grader A's 'roughly a quarter' adoption figure was unsourced; the Fed figure is 46% for any mobile payment.

Both graders agree the measurable clause held: central banks routinely publish big-data nowcasts (Atlanta Fed GDPNow from 2014, NY Fed nowcast) with alternative-data and ML inputs. Under D22/D27 an unmeasurable clause is not graded; it cannot count against the view. Grader A downgraded to partial for the ungraded value clause, which mixes the two rules. Note: the factual clause is shared by option B, so the hit says little about the panel's real split.

BLS chart confirms US unemployment 4.0-4.4% Jan-Sep 2025, but aggregate unemployment does not measure jobs displaced vs created by AI and robots; no public series measures that balance, so the evidence is a proxy of another quantity (D22/D23) and supports neither hit nor miss.

Read 'at the levels of tens of billions' as an order of magnitude, the dominant reading of a definitional threshold. NotPetya (2017), a Russian military operation, disabled Ukrainian ministries, banks, metro, energy and telecoms and caused over $10B in damage per the White House. That meets both the national-security and the scale test, at the lower edge. Grader B's partial rests on reading 'tens' as at least $20B; defensible but the narrower reading.

The option is an explicit comparison with early 2020, not a counterfactual (the counterfactual is the third option), so it is measurable on population-level wellbeing. Global HDI hit a record high in 2023 and kept rising; Gallup's 2024 global thriving median (33%) is higher than before the pandemic and suffering (7%) matches the record low. Life was not mostly worse for most people. Uneven recovery in about half of LDCs affects a minority of people.
